newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland must brace for rain, new floods, PM says.
newsitem.headline: Poland must brace for rain, new floods, PM says.

text.p: Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz warned Poland on Thursday that forecast heavy rains could trigger more of the floods that have already killed 46 people and devastated huge areas of the south.
Cimoszewicz told parliament that weather forecasts predicted heavy rain overnight and into the weekend.

"We must expect the possiblity, unfortunately, of the start of another wave of floods," he told an emergency session of the lower house which had gathered on Wednesday to rush through 22 laws to deal with Poland's worst natural disaster for several centuries.
Poland's zloty currency, which lost five percent against a basket of currencies on Tuesday, then stabilised, jolted down again on Thursday after the premier's dramatic announcement.
Opposition parliamentarians, already savagely critical of government crisis management and scenting blood before elections on September 21, renewed their onslaught.
Cimoszewicz said he was drafting extra troops into endangered areas and urged residents, without panic, to prepare. "We must hope it will not happen, but let's be better prepared," he said.

Police put Poland's death toll so far at 46 in the current floods. Water has swamped 4,500 sq km (1,700 square miles), of which around two-fifths was still inundated. It has struck 40,000 farms, 86 towns and 875 villages.
The country has called a day of mourning for Friday.
If new floods come they will strike communities already exhausted and heartbroken by the ordeal so far.

Waters were only just receding in the south, leaving a stench and a risk of disease in shattered streets veiled in sewage, rubbish and dead animals. A wave of high water continued to advance on Thursday north along the Odra river and the German border, attacking new towns and villages.

Deputy farm minister Jerzy Pilarczyk left a session of the government crisis committee to tell Reuters that if the rain forecasts over the Odra river's Czech headwaters were correct, they could prompt floods similar to the latest ones.
He said the effects might be less severe as people would be better prepared. But the south and the major cities of Wroclaw and Opole, only just getting to their feet, might be hit again.

The forecast rain would only be half as heavy as that which prompted earlier floods. But the prime minister said because levels in rivers and reservoirs were still high, there was now less scope to absorb extra water.

Parliament carried on voting on bills to hasten aid and money to scenes of the disaster. These included measures changing the current budget to allow more borrowing at home and abroad, cash for affected households, and grain supplies to farmers.

Opposition parties charged the government, led by ex-communists, with incompetence but a motion on Thursday to reject the government's report explaining its crisis actions so far, was defeated by 231 votes to 98 with 30 abstentions.
The opposition particularly reproaches the cabinet for not declaring a state of emergency -- a move which Cimoszewicz says would do no good and delay the elections.

Cimoszewicz phoned Hungary's Prime Minister Gyula Horn and Poland appealed to Germany and Sweden for urgent help to face the new onslaught, PAP news agency reported. Poland's main needs include heavy-duty pumping gear.
As the government faced a massive task of urgent relief and longer-term reconstruction, it walked a tightrope between the need for resources and a danger of harming economic stability.

Finance minister Marek Belka tried to soothe frayed nerves on the country's currency market, telling public radio the zloty fall was not serious. "I watch it with calm...I think it will now reverse," he said just before the premier's statement.
But his words apparently did little to help the zloty, although Poland's share market, where few major firms have been directly affected, coolly rose.
